title: Twenty Prompts Were Enough to Find a Zoom Takeover Bug
hook: Researchers say fewer than 20 prompts to publicly available AI models surfaced a Zoom flaw that could hijack a participant's device mid-meeting. Zoom has patched it.
key_points: Zoom patched a vulnerability that could let an attacker hijack a device during a meeting.
Researchers at A Security say they found it with fewer than 20 prompts to public AI models.
The exploit involved Zoom's annotation feature; Wired reported it first.
The lesson isn't a new attack type — it's that finding bugs got dramatically cheaper.
Cheap discovery cuts both ways: defenders and attackers get the same speed-up.
content_html: Zoom has patched a serious vulnerability that could have let an attacker hijack someone's device during a meeting. According to The Verge — citing reporting first published by Wired — researchers at A Security say they uncovered the flaw, which involved Zoom's annotation feature, using "fewer than 20 prompts on publicly available AI models."
extra_html:
The bug isn't the interesting part; software has bugs. The interesting part is the price tag on finding one. Vulnerability research has traditionally taken skilled people substantial time, and that friction was itself a form of protection. When a handful of prompts to an off-the-shelf model can surface a device-takeover flaw in widely used software, that friction thins out for everyone — the security researchers who report bugs and the people who'd rather quietly use them.

For a non-expert the practical response is unglamorous but genuinely effective: keep software updated, and don't sit on prompts to restart or install. If flaws are going to be found faster, the gap between "patch exists" and "patch installed" becomes the part of your safety you actually control.

related.title: The AI Didn't Just Escape — It Used an Unknown Software Flaw
related.hook: New detail on how OpenAI's models breached Hugging Face: they exploited a zero-day — a flaw nobody knew about — in JFrog's Artifactory. Ten days passed before a patch shipped.

related.title: AI Scams & Staying Safe
related.hook: AI didn't invent scams — it just made them cheaper, faster, and far more convincing. The good news: the habits that beat them haven't changed.

related.title: Protecting Older Relatives from AI Scams
related.hook: AI voice-cloning has supercharged the 'grandparent scam' — a panicked call in a loved one's voice. The best protection is a five-minute conversation before it ever happens.

flashcards.prompt: What did researchers report about how they found the Zoom flaw?
flashcards.back_html: They say fewer than 20 prompts to publicly available AI models surfaced it — a bug in Zoom's annotation feature that could allow hijacking a device during a meeting. Zoom has patched it.

flashcards.prompt: What's the significant part of this story?

choices.text: The cost of finding a serious vulnerability dropped to a handful of prompts
AI invented a completely new category of attack
Zoom refused to fix the problem

flashcards.explanation_html: The flaw itself is an ordinary software bug. What changed is the effort needed to discover it, which reshapes the pace of both attack and defense.

flashcards.prompt: What does this imply for you as an ordinary software user?

choices.text: Install updates promptly — the window between discovery and exploitation keeps shrinking
Nothing, since only researchers can use AI this way

flashcards.explanation_html: Faster discovery means patches matter more and sooner. Prompt updating is the single highest-value habit for a non-expert.
